stem: After the storm surge crested, floodwaters began to _____, allowing residents to return to their homes by nightfall.
explain: Clue: waters receded, letting people return. abate/subside mean to decrease. escalate/intensify (opposite trap) wrongly suggest worsening.

stem: Climbing the unmarked ridge in a whiteout proved so _____ that two members of the expedition turned back before reaching base camp.
explain: Clue: climbers turned back. arduous/onerous mean extremely difficult. effortless/facile (trap pair) wrongly mean easy.

stem: The new intern's _____ manner toward every executive, bowing and offering unsolicited praise, embarrassed his more independent-minded colleagues.
explain: Clue: bowing, unsolicited praise. obsequious/servile mean overly submissive. haughty/imperious (trap pair) wrongly mean arrogant.

stem: Unlike the redwood's centuries-long life span, the mayfly's existence is _____, lasting only a single day.
explain: Clue: 'unlike' the redwood, lasting one day. ephemeral/transient mean short-lived. permanent/enduring (trap pair) wrongly mean lasting.

stem: Despite the reporter's persistent questioning, the scientist remained _____, offering only clipped one-word replies.
explain: Clue: clipped one-word replies despite questioning. reticent/taciturn mean reserved in speech. garrulous/loquacious (trap pair) wrongly mean talkative.

stem: The archivist's _____ attention to every faded date and marginal note made her catalog the most reliable in the collection.
explain: Clue: attention to every faded detail produced the most reliable catalog. meticulous/punctilious mean extremely careful. careless/slipshod (trap) wrongly mean sloppy.

stem: In contrast to his predecessor's flowery speeches, the new president delivered a _____ address of barely two minutes.
explain: Clue: 'in contrast' to flowery, only two minutes. laconic/terse mean using few words. verbose/loquacious (trap) wrongly mean wordy.

stem: The negotiator hoped a modest concession would _____ the striking workers before the talks collapsed entirely.
explain: Clue: a concession meant to prevent collapse of talks. placate/appease mean to calm. provoke/incite (trap) wrongly mean to anger.

stem: Although the mushroom's bright color suggested danger, mycologists confirmed it was entirely _____.
explain: Clue: 'although' color suggested danger, but scientists found otherwise. innocuous/harmless mean not dangerous. noxious/deleterious (trap) wrongly mean harmful.

stem: The child's _____ account of the accident, offered without a hint of self-interest, convinced the jury more than any adult testimony.
explain: Clue: no self-interest, most convincing. guileless/artless mean honest and without cunning. disingenuous/duplicitous (trap) wrongly mean deceitful.

stem: The unexpected bequest left the small museum with a _____ of artifacts, far more than its storage rooms could hold.
explain: Clue: far more than storage could hold. plethora/cornucopia mean an abundance. paucity/dearth (trap) wrongly mean a scarcity.

stem: Decades of drought and crop failure left the farming community in such _____ that many families could not afford basic staples.
explain: Clue: could not afford staples. indigence/penury mean extreme poverty. affluence/opulence (trap) wrongly mean wealth.

stem: The rookie pilot's _____ decision to fly directly into the thunderhead alarmed even the most experienced crew members.
explain: Clue: alarmed experienced crew, so the decision was recklessly bold. audacious/brazen mean boldly daring. timorous/diffident (trap) wrongly mean timid.

stem: The two rival startups eventually _____ into a single firm, pooling their patents and staff.
explain: Clue: pooling patents and staff into one firm. amalgamated/coalesced mean combined. diverged/splintered (trap) wrongly mean split apart.

stem: Reviewers noted a glaring _____ between the film's lavish marketing budget and its threadbare production values.
explain: Clue: 'glaring' mismatch between budget and quality. discrepancy/incongruity mean a mismatch. correspondence/conformity (trap) wrongly mean agreement.

stem: Even on the day of his promotion, the manager remained _____, rarely smiling and dismissing every congratulation with a shrug.
explain: Clue: rarely smiling despite good news. morose/saturnine mean gloomy. ebullient/jubilant (trap) wrongly mean joyful.

stem: The waxed fabric proved _____ to rain, so the campers stayed dry through the entire storm.
explain: Clue: stayed dry through the storm. impervious/impermeable mean unable to be penetrated. porous/permeable (trap) wrongly mean allowing liquid through.

stem: Because the rescued dog was remarkably _____, trainers were able to teach it basic commands within a week.
explain: Clue: quickly trained. tractable/amenable mean easily managed. recalcitrant/obdurate (trap) wrongly mean stubborn.

stem: Even as the courtroom erupted in shouting, the judge remained _____, her expression betraying nothing.
explain: Clue: expression betraying nothing amid chaos. imperturbable/phlegmatic mean calm and unaffected. distraught/frantic (trap) wrongly mean agitated.

stem: The harvest that year was so _____ that the granary had to be expanded to store the surplus grain.
explain: Clue: surplus grain, needed expanded storage. copious/abundant mean plentiful. meager/scanty (trap) wrongly mean scarce.

stem: The philosophy seminar's central texts were so _____ that even advanced graduate students needed a glossary to follow the argument.
explain: Clue: even advanced students needed a glossary. recondite/esoteric mean obscure and hard to understand. elementary/rudimentary (trap) wrongly mean basic.

stem: The lecture's monotone delivery was so _____ that half the class had dozed off by the second slide.
explain: Clue: half the class dozed off. soporific/somnolent mean sleep-inducing. invigorating/bracing (trap) wrongly mean energizing.

stem: The technician was so _____ in checking each solder joint that the final circuit board contained not a single defect.
explain: Clue: not a single defect resulted. assiduous/sedulous mean diligent and careful. cursory/perfunctory (trap) wrongly mean hasty.

stem: Because the coral reef's limestone skeleton is highly _____, seawater and dissolved nutrients pass easily through its structure.
explain: Clue: water passes easily through. porous/permeable mean full of tiny openings. impervious/impenetrable (trap) wrongly mean blocking passage.

stem: The tabloid's account of the senator's remarks was so _____ that it bore almost no resemblance to what she actually said.
explain: Clue: bore almost no resemblance to what she actually said. fabricated/concocted mean invented, made up rather than accurate. veracious/candid (trap) wrongly mean truthful; pastoral/torpid are unrelated distractors (rural; sluggish).

stem: Once known for prudent budgeting, the town council grew increasingly _____, approving lavish projects with little regard for cost.
explain: Clue: lavish spending with little regard for cost. profligate/prodigal mean wastefully extravagant. frugal/parsimonious (trap) wrongly mean thrifty.

stem: The museum guide's _____ commentary, crammed with dates, dynasties, and obscure trivia, left visitors more confused than informed.
explain: Clue: crammed with dates, dynasties, and obscure trivia, leaving visitors confused rather than informed. pedantic/professorial mean overly concerned with minute, bookish detail at the expense of clarity. succinct/pithy (trap) wrongly mean concise; riparian/littoral (relating to riverbanks/shorelines) are irrelevant distractors.

stem: The comedian's set was so _____ that even the most straight-laced audience members were doubled over with laughter.
explain: Clue: even the most straight-laced audience members were doubled over with laughter. droll/jocose mean amusingly playful, comic. somber/lugubrious (trap) wrongly mean gloomy; alpine/equatorial are irrelevant geographic distractors.

stem: The delegation's demand for immediate surrender, with no room for negotiation, was widely condemned as _____.
explain: Clue: no room for negotiation. peremptory/imperious mean allowing no refusal, commanding. conciliatory/accommodating (trap) wrongly mean willing to compromise.

stem: The critic praised the debut novel's _____ prose, noting that not a single sentence felt superfluous or unclear.
explain: Clue: not a single sentence unclear. lucid/pellucid mean clear and easily understood. turbid/murky (trap) wrongly mean unclear.

stem: The senator's speech was riddled with _____ claims that, though superficially persuasive, collapsed under the slightest logical scrutiny.
explain: Clue: superficially persuasive but collapse under scrutiny. specious/fallacious mean seemingly sound but actually false. cogent/valid (trap) wrongly mean genuinely convincing.

stem: The union representative refused to _____ his position, even after management offered a substantial raise.
explain: Clue: refused despite an incentive to change. recant/abjure mean to retract or formally reject a prior stance. reaffirm/reiterate (trap) wrongly mean to restate the same position.

stem: The editorial's tone was so _____ that readers assumed the author bore the mayor a personal grudge.
explain: Clue: readers assumed personal animosity. vituperative/caustic mean bitterly abusive. laudatory/encomiastic (trap) wrongly mean praising.

stem: Because the treaty's terms were left deliberately _____, each signatory nation later interpreted the wording to its own advantage.
explain: Clue: each nation interpreted the wording differently. ambiguous/equivocal mean open to multiple meanings. explicit/unequivocal (trap) wrongly mean perfectly clear.

stem: The dean's _____ manner toward faculty concerns, always listening but never acting, eventually eroded the department's trust in her leadership.
explain: Clue: listening but never acting eroded trust. perfunctory/cursory mean done with minimal effort or genuine interest. assiduous/sedulous (trap) wrongly mean diligent.

stem: Long before the invention of antibiotics, physicians could do little more than _____ the patient's fever, since the underlying infection remained untreatable.
explain: Clue: relieving symptoms since a cure was unavailable. mitigate/alleviate mean to lessen severity. exacerbate/aggravate (trap) wrongly mean to worsen.

stem: Historians once dismissed the border skirmishes as minor, but new archives reveal they were in fact _____ to the empire's eventual collapse.
explain: Clue: 'in fact' contradicts 'minor' — the skirmishes actually mattered greatly. instrumental/pivotal mean crucially important. incidental/tangential (trap) wrongly mean of minor relevance.

stem: The philanthropist's donations, though generous in appearance, were calculated with such _____ that every dollar bought her a tax advantage.
explain: Clue: every dollar calculated for advantage. shrewdness/cunning mean cleverness in self-interest. naivete/ingenuousness (trap) wrongly mean innocence.

stem: The committee's report was praised for its _____ prose, which distilled a decade of dense economic data into a few clear paragraphs.
explain: Clue: distilled dense data into clear paragraphs. lucid/cogent mean clear and well-reasoned. convoluted/labyrinthine (trap) wrongly mean complicated.

stem: The old professor's lectures were famously _____, wandering from the assigned topic into decades-old anecdotes before anyone could redirect him.
explain: Clue: wandering off topic into anecdotes. desultory/digressive mean lacking a fixed plan, straying. methodical/systematic (trap) wrongly mean orderly.

stem: The defense attorney's closing argument was so _____ that even skeptical jurors, unable to find any flaw in its logic, found themselves nodding in agreement.
explain: Clue: skeptical jurors could find no flaw in the argument's logic, meaning it was genuinely sound, not just superficially convincing. cogent/persuasive mean genuinely compelling and well-reasoned. specious/fallacious (trap) wrongly mean deceptively plausible but flawed — ruled out because the added clue confirms the logic held up under scrutiny.

stem: The senator's opponents accused her of being _____, changing her position on the tariff bill three times within a single month.
explain: Clue: changed position three times. vacillating/irresolute mean wavering between choices. steadfast/resolute (trap) wrongly mean firm and unchanging.

stem: Rather than confront the allegations directly, the executive issued a statement so _____ that reporters could not tell whether he was admitting or denying wrongdoing.
explain: Clue: reporters could not tell what he meant. vague/indeterminate mean deliberately unclear. categorical/unequivocal (trap) wrongly mean stated without doubt.

stem: The critic's review was notably _____, praising the cinematography while ignoring the film's incoherent plot entirely.
explain: Clue: praising one aspect while ignoring flaws shows one-sidedness. partial/biased mean favoring one side unfairly. impartial/disinterested (trap) wrongly mean objective.

stem: The archaeologist's initial hypothesis proved _____ once carbon dating revealed the artifacts were centuries older than she had assumed.
explain: Clue: new evidence undermined the hypothesis. untenable/indefensible mean unable to be defended. corroborated/substantiated (trap) wrongly mean confirmed.

stem: The chemistry professor warned that the compound was highly _____, capable of igniting at the slightest spark.
explain: Clue: capable of igniting at the slightest spark. volatile/unstable mean prone to sudden, violent change. inert/stable (trap) wrongly mean unreactive.

stem: The novel's protagonist is portrayed as _____, incapable of settling on a single career or even a permanent address.
explain: Clue: incapable of settling on anything. indecisive/wavering mean unable to commit to a single course. steadfast/unwavering (trap) wrongly mean firmly committed.

stem: Far from being a spontaneous uprising, the coup was in fact the product of months of _____ plotting among disaffected officers.
explain: Clue: 'far from spontaneous' — carefully hidden planning. clandestine/covert mean secret. overt/public (trap) wrongly mean done openly.

stem: The retired diplomat's memoir was praised for its _____ candor, sparing no embarrassing detail about his own failures.
explain: Clue: sparing no embarrassing detail. unflinching/forthright mean direct and honest without reservation. guarded/circumspect (trap) wrongly mean cautious and reserved.

stem: The economist's forecast proved _____, since actual growth figures matched her projections almost to the decimal point.
explain: Clue: figures matched projections almost exactly. prescient/accurate mean correctly foreseeing outcomes. erroneous/fallacious (trap) wrongly mean mistaken.

stem: The city council's plan to raze the historic district met with such _____ opposition that the project was shelved within weeks.
explain: Clue: opposition strong enough to shelve the project quickly. vociferous/strident mean loud and forceful. muted/subdued (trap) wrongly mean quiet.

stem: The tribal chief's authority was considered _____, deriving not from any written law but from generations of unquestioned custom.
explain: Clue: authority arose from within custom, not from outside law. inherent/intrinsic mean belonging naturally to something. extraneous/extrinsic (trap) wrongly mean coming from outside.

stem: Despite decades of research, the origins of the ritual remain _____, with scholars offering only speculative reconstructions.
explain: Clue: only speculative reconstructions exist. obscure/recondite mean unclear or hidden from understanding. manifest/self-evident (trap) wrongly mean obvious.

stem: The startup's founders were so _____ about market risk that they refused even routine insurance, convinced that failure was impossible.
explain: Clue: refused insurance, convinced failure impossible. sanguine/insouciant mean unworried, optimistic to a fault. apprehensive/trepidatious (trap) wrongly mean fearful.

stem: The senator's rhetoric grew increasingly _____ as the campaign wore on, each speech more inflated with grandiose promises than the last.
explain: Clue: each speech more inflated with grand promises. bombastic/grandiloquent mean pompously inflated in language. understated/restrained (trap) wrongly mean modest.

stem: The witness's testimony was so _____ that the prosecution could find no inconsistency to exploit under cross-examination.
explain: Clue: no inconsistency to exploit. consistent/coherent mean logically unified. disjointed/incongruous (trap) wrongly mean disconnected.

stem: Rather than confront her rival directly, the queen preferred _____ methods, spreading rumors through intermediaries who could never be traced back to her.
explain: Clue: through intermediaries, never traced back. clandestine/surreptitious mean secretive and hidden. forthright/candid (trap) wrongly mean open and direct.

stem: The mathematician's proof, though only two pages long, was so _____ that specialists spent years verifying every step.
explain: Clue: took years to verify a short proof. dense/intricate mean complex and tightly packed with meaning. simplistic/facile (trap) wrongly mean overly simple.

stem: The colony's isolation bred a fiercely _____ culture, suspicious of outsiders and resistant to any foreign custom.
explain: Clue: suspicious of outsiders, resistant to foreign custom. insular/parochial mean narrow-minded and isolated. cosmopolitan/worldly (trap) wrongly mean open to other cultures.

stem: The panel's decision, reached without consulting any of the affected employees, struck many as _____ .
explain: Clue: reached without consultation. arbitrary/capricious mean based on whim rather than reason. judicious/considered (trap) wrongly mean carefully reasoned.

stem: The curator's essay was criticized as _____, offering sweeping judgments about the artist's genius without a single supporting citation.
explain: Clue: sweeping judgments with no citation. unsubstantiated/unfounded mean lacking evidence. documented/corroborated (trap) wrongly mean backed by evidence.

stem: The board's decision to slash research funding, despite record profits, struck shareholders as remarkably _____ .
explain: Clue: cutting funding despite record profits seems unwise. imprudent/injudicious mean unwise, lacking good judgment. prudent/judicious (trap) wrongly mean wise.

stem: The senator's apology was widely seen as _____, offered only after polling data revealed the scandal was costing her support.
explain: Clue: timed to polling data, not genuine remorse. expedient/calculated mean done for strategic advantage. spontaneous/unpremeditated (trap) wrongly mean unplanned.

stem: The professor's marginal comments were so _____ that students often needed a second reader just to decipher his handwriting and meaning.
explain: Clue: needed a second reader to decipher. cryptic/inscrutable mean mysteriously hard to interpret. transparent/perspicuous (trap) wrongly mean easily understood.

stem: The negotiations stalled because both delegations proved equally _____, refusing to yield a single clause of the draft agreement.
explain: Clue: refused to yield anything. intransigent/obdurate mean stubbornly unyielding. conciliatory/accommodating (trap) wrongly mean willing to compromise.

stem: The choir director insisted on _____ precision, stopping rehearsal at the slightest deviation from the printed score.
explain: Clue: stopped at the slightest deviation. rigorous/exacting mean demanding strict, precise adherence to a standard. cursory/slapdash (trap) wrongly mean careless.

stem: Once a fervent believer, the philosopher grew increasingly _____ in later life, doubting even claims he had once considered self-evident.
explain: Clue: doubting former certainties. skeptical/doubtful mean inclined to question. credulous/gullible (trap) wrongly mean readily believing.

stem: The band's early recordings sound remarkably _____ today, their once-shocking dissonance now a familiar feature of mainstream pop.
explain: Clue: once-shocking sound now familiar/mainstream, i.e., no longer novel. hackneyed/unoriginal mean stale and trite from overuse. innovative/groundbreaking (trap) wrongly mean pioneering.

stem: Because the soil beneath the site was so _____, engineers had to reinforce the foundation against constant seepage.
explain: Clue: constant seepage requiring reinforcement. waterlogged/saturated mean thoroughly soaked with water. impermeable/impervious (trap) wrongly mean blocking water entirely; arid wrongly suggests dryness.

stem: The senator's remarks, though brief, were _____ enough to reshape the entire debate over the pipeline.
explain: Clue: brief remarks reshaped an entire debate — high impact. consequential/momentous mean highly significant. negligible/trifling (trap) wrongly mean unimportant.

stem: The old bridge's rusted supports were judged _____ by inspectors, who closed it to traffic the same afternoon.
explain: Clue: closed to traffic immediately. unsound/precarious mean structurally unsafe. sturdy/robust (trap) wrongly mean strong and reliable.

stem: The city's new zoning laws were so _____ that developers found loopholes within days of their passage.
explain: Clue: developers found loopholes within days. lax/permissive mean insufficiently strict. stringent/rigorous (trap) wrongly mean strict.

stem: The playwright's dialogue was praised for being _____, each line advancing the plot without a single wasted word.
explain: Clue: not a single wasted word. economical/spare mean using minimal, efficient language. verbose/prolix (trap) wrongly mean wordy.

stem: Long dismissed as a fringe theory, the hypothesis gained _____ support after new fossil evidence emerged.
explain: Clue: new evidence changed the theory's standing from fringe to accepted. considerable/substantial mean sizable. negligible/scant (trap) wrongly mean very little.

stem: The court's ruling was so narrowly _____ that it resolved the immediate dispute while leaving the broader constitutional question entirely untouched.
explain: Clue: resolved only the immediate dispute, left broader question untouched. circumscribed/delimited mean narrowly limited in scope. sweeping/comprehensive (trap) wrongly mean broad in scope.

stem: The monarch's edicts, once accepted without question, came to seem increasingly _____ as literacy spread and subjects began to scrutinize the law's rationale.
explain: Clue: subjects began scrutinizing rationale, implying the edicts lacked one. baseless/groundless mean lacking any rational foundation. warranted/justified (trap) wrongly mean reasonably supported.

stem: The philosopher's late writings grew so _____ that even his most devoted disciples debated for decades over what he actually meant.
explain: Clue: disciples debated for decades over meaning. inscrutable/impenetrable mean impossible to fathom. perspicuous/lucid (trap) wrongly mean clearly expressed.

stem: The regime's propaganda relied less on outright falsehood than on _____ euphemism, reframing atrocities in language bland enough to pass unnoticed.
explain: Clue: bland language meant to pass unnoticed, not shocking. anodyne/innocuous mean mild and inoffensive. inflammatory/incendiary (trap) wrongly mean provocative.

stem: The critic argued that the sculptor's late work, far from marking a decline, in fact achieved a mastery of form so _____ that his earlier, more derivative pieces never approached it.
explain: Clue: 'far from decline,' surpassing earlier derivative work. consummate/peerless mean supremely skilled. rudimentary/nascent (trap) wrongly mean undeveloped.

stem: The treaty's negotiators, wary of appearing weak to their constituents, larded the final document with _____ language that promised much while committing to nothing.
explain: Clue: promised much while committing to nothing. noncommittal/evasive mean deliberately avoiding a firm commitment. categorical/forthright (trap) wrongly mean stated plainly and directly.

stem: Far from the austere ascetic later legend made him out to be, the hermit, contemporaries recorded, was in fact rather _____ in his tastes, keeping a well-stocked cellar and fine linens.
explain: Clue: 'far from austere ascetic,' well-stocked cellar and fine linens. epicurean/sybaritic mean devoted to luxury and pleasure. abstemious/ascetic (trap) wrongly mean self-denying.

stem: The economist's model, though elegant on paper, proved _____ once applied to real markets, its predictions diverging wildly from observed prices.
explain: Clue: predictions diverged wildly from reality. untenable/specious mean superficially plausible but flawed. robust/sound (trap) wrongly mean reliably valid.

stem: The senator's famously _____ style, dense with subordinate clauses and Latinate vocabulary, alienated an electorate accustomed to plainer speech.
explain: Clue: dense with ornate clauses, alienated plain-speaking voters. florid/grandiloquent mean elaborately ornate. austere/spare (trap) wrongly mean plain.

stem: Although the committee's final report reads as a model of consensus, internal memos reveal that its conclusions were reached only after weeks of _____ disagreement among the members.
explain: Clue: internal memos reveal hidden conflict beneath the polished report. acrimonious/vituperative mean bitterly hostile. amicable/cordial (trap) wrongly mean friendly.

stem: The novelist's prose style, once condemned as needlessly _____, is now celebrated by critics for the very density that earlier readers found impenetrable.
explain: Clue: once impenetrable, dense. convoluted/labyrinthine mean intricately complex. limpid/pellucid (trap) wrongly mean clear.

stem: Rather than temper her critique for a hostile audience, the scholar delivered a rebuttal so _____ that it left no assumption of her opponents unchallenged.
explain: Clue: no assumption left unchallenged, rather than tempering critique. trenchant/incisive mean sharply penetrating and forceful. equivocal/tepid (trap) wrongly mean vague or weak.

stem: The diplomat's memoirs reveal a man far more _____ than his stern public image suggested, prone to private jokes and unguarded affection with his staff.
explain: Clue: 'far more' than stern image, private jokes and affection. genial/convivial mean warmly sociable. dour/saturnine (trap) wrongly mean gloomy.

stem: The tribunal's ruling was criticized as _____, since it rested on precedents the judges themselves later admitted did not actually apply to the case.
explain: Clue: judges admitted the precedents did not apply. unsound/unfounded mean lacking valid basis. cogent/sound (trap) wrongly mean logically valid.

stem: The biographer resisted the temptation to _____ her subject's failures, instead documenting his cruelties with the same unsparing detail she gave his triumphs.
explain: Clue: documented cruelties with unsparing detail rather than softening them. gloss over/extenuate mean to minimize or excuse faults. expose/highlight (trap) wrongly mean to reveal prominently.

stem: The satirist's wit was never merely playful; beneath the jokes lay a _____ contempt for the politicians he lampooned.
explain: Clue: 'never merely playful,' contempt beneath the jokes. trenchant/mordant mean sharply, bitingly critical. benign/genial (trap) wrongly mean kind.

stem: The physicist's early papers were dismissed as _____ speculation, yet decades later their central claims were confirmed by direct observation.
explain: Clue: dismissed at first, only later confirmed — implying they seemed unfounded. fanciful/quixotic mean impractically idealistic, not grounded. empirical/evidence-based (trap) wrongly mean based on observation.

stem: The senator's opponents accused her of _____, pointing out that she had voted for the very regulations she now denounced on the campaign trail.
explain: Clue: denounces what she once voted for — contradicting herself. hypocrisy/duplicity mean saying one thing while doing another. consistency/constancy (trap) wrongly mean steadfastness.

stem: The playwright's late tragedies are marked by a despair so _____ that they offer audiences no consoling resolution, only the bare fact of suffering.
explain: Clue: no consoling resolution, only bare suffering. unmitigated/unrelieved mean not softened in any way. tempered/assuaged (trap) wrongly mean lessened.

stem: The anthropologist warned against _____ conclusions drawn from a single village, since regional customs varied so widely across the archipelago.
explain: Clue: warning implies conclusions were drawn too quickly given wide variation. hasty/precipitate mean rushed, drawn without sufficient basis. measured/circumspect (trap) wrongly mean careful.

stem: The reviewer noted that the orchestra's interpretation, while technically flawless, remained curiously _____, as though the musicians had memorized emotion rather than felt it.
explain: Clue: technically flawless yet lacking real feeling. bloodless/anemic mean lifeless, lacking vitality. impassioned/fervent (trap) wrongly mean full of feeling.

stem: The minister's resignation letter, though outwardly gracious, functioned as an attack so _____ that few colleagues recognized it as such until much later.
explain: Clue: outwardly gracious but actually critical — hidden, not open. veiled/oblique mean indirect, disguised. overt/blatant (trap) wrongly mean openly obvious.

stem: The historian's account of the famine has been criticized as _____, minimizing the government's culpability while dwelling at length on natural causes.
explain: Clue: minimizing culpability while emphasizing other causes shows bias. tendentious/partisan mean promoting a particular slanted viewpoint. impartial/evenhanded (trap) wrongly mean unbiased.

stem: The composer's late quartets, once considered forbiddingly _____, are now standard fare in conservatory repertoire.
explain: Clue: 'once forbidding,' now standard/accessible repertoire implies originally hard to grasp. abstruse/impenetrable mean very difficult to understand. accessible/approachable (trap) wrongly mean easy to engage with.

stem: The ambassador's toast, larded with diplomatic _____, left both delegations unsure whether an actual concession had been offered.
explain: Clue: unsure whether a concession was offered — indirect, roundabout language. circumlocution/periphrasis mean indirect, wordy expression avoiding directness. candor/forthrightness (trap) wrongly mean directness.

stem: The critic dismissed the memoir as _____, its author apparently more concerned with cultivating a legend than with recording events as they occurred.
explain: Clue: cultivating a legend about oneself rather than accuracy. self-aggrandizing/vainglorious mean promoting one's own greatness. self-deprecating/modest (trap) wrongly mean humble.

stem: The museum's new wing, far from being an eyesore, proved a remarkably _____ addition that harmonized with the original facade.
explain: Clue: 'far from...proved' signals a positive, well-fitting word; predict 'fitting.' Felicitous means well-chosen. Trap: ostentatious sounds architectural but means showy, the wrong direction.

stem: Because the professor's lecture wandered from topic to topic with no discernible plan, students found it _____ and difficult to follow.
explain: Clue: 'wandered...no discernible plan' predicts 'rambling.' Desultory means random and disconnected. Trap: laconic (brief) describes length, not lack of structure.

stem: Although the senator publicly praised her rival's bill, her private memos revealed a deep _____ toward the legislation.
explain: 'Although...publicly praised' versus private memos signals contrast; predict 'dislike.' Antipathy fits. Trap: affinity is the opposite direction, a false contrast-reversal.

stem: Weakened by decades of rust, the old bridge finally became so _____ that engineers closed it to all traffic.
explain: 'Weakened...closed to traffic' predicts 'unsafe.' Precarious means risky. Trap: sturdy is a direct opposite that a careless reader might associate with bridges.

stem: Unlike his gregarious brother, Tomas was notoriously _____, preferring solitary walks to crowded parties.
explain: 'Unlike gregarious...solitary' predicts 'withdrawn.' Reticent means reserved. Trap: garrulous (talkative) is thematically related to sociability but is the wrong direction.

stem: The committee's report offered _____ detail, covering every line item of the budget across nearly four hundred pages.
explain: 'Every line item...four hundred pages' predicts 'abundant.' Copious means plentiful. Trap: cursory (superficial) is thematically related to reports but signals the opposite thoroughness.

stem: Because the evidence against the defendant was purely circumstantial, the prosecutor's case remained _____ at best.
explain: 'Purely circumstantial' predicts 'weak.' Tenuous means insubstantial. Trap: cogent (convincing) is the opposite of what flimsy evidence supports.

stem: Even after losing the championship, the coach remained _____, refusing to let the defeat dampen his optimism.
explain: 'Refusing to let defeat dampen his optimism' predicts 'enthusiastic.' Ebullient fits. Trap: morose (sullen) is the opposite, tempting after a loss.

stem: The professor's explanations were so _____ that even students unfamiliar with the subject grasped the concept at once.
explain: 'Grasped the concept at once' predicts 'clear.' Pellucid means easily understood. Trap: recondite (obscure) is the direct opposite, wrongly tempting for 'explanations of a subject.'

stem: The senator's speech, larded with grandiose promises and inflated phrasing, struck many listeners as _____ rather than sincere.
explain: 'Grandiose...inflated phrasing' predicts 'pompous.' Bombastic fits. Trap: laconic (using few words) contradicts the description of inflated phrasing.

stem: The company's new policy, though initially unpopular, proved _____ once employees saw how much time it actually saved them.
explain: 'Though initially unpopular...saved them time' signals reversal; predict 'beneficial.' Salutary fits. Trap: onerous (burdensome) matches the initial unpopularity but ignores the 'though' reversal.

stem: Critics dismissed the film's plot as utterly _____, a hodgepodge of clichés stitched together with no coherent structure.
explain: 'Hodgepodge...no coherent structure' predicts 'fragmented.' Disjointed fits exactly. Trap: homogeneous is thematically about unity but means uniform, not the intended meaning here.

stem: Despite years of drought, the region's ancient irrigation canals kept the fields _____, yielding crops even in the driest summers.
explain: 'Despite drought...yielding crops' predicts 'well-watered.' Saturated fits. Trap: fallow (unsown) is thematically about farmland but contradicts 'yielding crops.'

stem: The young intern's _____ questions revealed how little experience she had, yet her supervisors found her eagerness endearing.
explain: 'How little experience' predicts 'naive.' Ingenuous means naive and trusting. Trap: erudite (learned) is the opposite, though it might tempt someone focused only on 'intern' and 'questions.'

stem: Rather than confront his mistake directly, the manager offered only a _____ apology that satisfied no one.
explain: 'Rather than confront...satisfied no one' predicts 'insincere/superficial.' Perfunctory fits. Trap: contrite (genuinely sorry) is thematically about apology but implies real remorse.

stem: The old sailor's stories, though entertaining, were so _____ that no one could tell fact from exaggeration.
explain: 'No one could tell fact from exaggeration' predicts 'exaggerated/decorated.' Embellished fits. Trap: austere (unadorned) is the opposite, describing plainness rather than decoration.

stem: Because the new medication reduced her symptoms almost immediately, the patient described its effect as remarkably _____.
explain: 'Reduced symptoms almost immediately' predicts 'health-giving.' Salubrious means healthful. Trap: noxious is thematically about medication's effects but means harmful, the opposite.

stem: The politician's promises were so vague that voters grew _____ of his ability to deliver real change.
explain: 'So vague' predicts 'doubtful.' Skeptical fits. Trap: credulous (easily fooled) is thematically about belief but is the opposite reaction to vague promises.

stem: The abandoned house, untouched for decades, remained surprisingly _____, its original furnishings still intact.
explain: 'Surprisingly...furnishings still intact' predicts 'unspoiled.' Pristine fits. Trap: dilapidated is thematically expected for an abandoned house but contradicts 'intact.'

stem: The negotiator's _____ manner put both sides at ease, allowing the talks to proceed without hostility.
explain: 'Put both sides at ease...without hostility' predicts 'peace-making.' Conciliatory fits. Trap: contentious (quarrelsome) is thematically about negotiation but signals conflict, the opposite.

stem: Because the professor never varied his tone or paused for questions, his lecture felt _____ rather than engaging.
explain: 'Never varied his tone' predicts 'dull, flat.' Vapid means dull and lacking flavor or spirit. Trap: animated is thematically about lecture delivery but is the opposite of unvarying.

stem: The chef's dishes, once praised for bold flavor, had grown _____ after years of the same uninspired recipes.
explain: 'Once bold...same uninspired recipes' signals decline; predict 'bland.' Insipid fits. Trap: piquant (pleasantly pungent) is thematically about flavor but is the opposite of bland.

stem: The witness's account was so _____ that the jury had no trouble believing every detail.
explain: 'No trouble believing' predicts 'truthful.' Veracious means truthful, accurate. Trap: specious (seemingly logical but false) is thematically about testimony but implies the account was actually misleading.

stem: The volunteers worked with such _____ that the shelter was rebuilt in half the expected time.
explain: 'Rebuilt in half the expected time' predicts 'eager speed.' Alacrity fits. Trap: lassitude (sluggishness) is thematically about work pace but is the opposite of fast progress.

stem: The child's excuse was so _____ that even her parents, eager to believe her, could not accept it.
explain: 'Even her parents, eager to believe her, could not accept it' predicts 'unbelievable.' Implausible fits. Trap: plausible is the opposite, tempting because it sounds similar.

stem: The historian argued that the treaty's failure was not the result of any single miscalculation but rather an accumulation of small, _____ errors over many years.
explain: 'Not...but rather an accumulation...over many years' predicts 'occasional, scattered.' Sporadic fits. Trap: deliberate is thematically about errors but implies intent, contradicting 'accumulation of small errors.'

stem: Though the diplomat's tone remained calm throughout the summit, his written proposals were laced with _____ that hinted at underlying contempt for his counterparts.
explain: 'Calm tone' versus written proposals 'hinted at contempt' signals contrast; predict 'abuse.' Invective means verbal abuse. Trap: platitudes (stale phrases) is thematically diplomatic but doesn't convey contempt.

stem: Rather than confront the flaws in his theory directly, the scientist resorted to _____ language whenever a colleague raised objections.
explain: 'Rather than confront directly...resorted to' predicts 'evasive.' Equivocal fits. Trap: forthright is the opposite, describing directness rather than evasion.

stem: The novel's ending, which many readers found unsatisfying, was in fact carefully _____ by the author from the very first chapter.
explain: 'In fact carefully...from the very first chapter' signals a reversal of expectation toward 'planned/hinted at.' Presaged means indicated in advance. Trap: concealed is thematically related but implies hiding rather than early hinting.

stem: Despite his reputation for _____ remarks, the critic's review of the young poet's debut was surprisingly gentle.
explain: 'Despite his reputation for...surprisingly gentle' signals contrast; predict 'harsh.' Caustic fits. Trap: laudatory (praising) matches the review's actual tone but contradicts the required contrast word for 'reputation.'

stem: The economist's forecast, hedged with countless qualifications, was so _____ that policymakers could draw no clear conclusions from it.
explain: 'Hedged with countless qualifications...no clear conclusions' predicts 'ambiguous.' Equivocal fits. Trap: categorical (absolute) is the opposite of hedged language.

stem: The archivist's meticulous cataloguing system, once considered _____, is now standard practice in libraries worldwide.
explain: 'Once considered...now standard practice' signals the system was formerly unconventional; predict 'radical.' Iconoclastic fits. Trap: conventional describes its current status, not its original reputation.

stem: The senator's opponents accused her of _____, noting that her voting record contradicted nearly every promise from her campaign.
explain: 'Voting record contradicted nearly every promise' predicts 'insincerity.' Disingenuousness fits. Trap: probity (honesty) is the opposite of the accusation implied by the contradiction.

stem: Although the committee's final report appeared _____, its conclusions were in fact based on rigorous years-long analysis.
explain: 'Although...appeared X, in fact based on rigorous analysis' signals contrast; predict 'haphazard-looking.' Desultory fits. Trap: systematic describes the actual underlying process, contradicting the required 'appeared' contrast.

stem: The biologist's data, far from confirming her hypothesis, actually _____ it, forcing her to abandon years of research.
explain: 'Far from confirming...forcing her to abandon' predicts 'contradicted.' Belied fits. Trap: corroborated is a near-synonym of the wrongly-expected 'confirmed,' the opposite of the actual outcome.

stem: The playwright's dialogue, though praised for its wit, was criticized by some as overly _____, favoring clever wordplay over genuine emotion.
explain: 'Favoring clever wordplay over genuine emotion' predicts 'joking, not serious.' Facetious fits. Trap: earnest is the opposite, describing genuine seriousness.

stem: The union leader's speech, intended to _____ striking workers, instead provoked further unrest among the crowd.
explain: 'Intended to X...instead provoked unrest' signals the intent was the opposite of the result; predict 'calm.' Placate fits. Trap: incite matches the actual outcome, not the stated intention.

stem: The board's decision, reached only after months of _____ debate, ultimately satisfied neither faction.
explain: 'Satisfied neither faction' after debate predicts 'quarrelsome.' Contentious fits. Trap: amicable (friendly) contradicts the unsatisfying, divisive outcome.

stem: The intern's _____ attention to every entry in the filing system impressed even the most demanding senior partners.
explain: 'Impressed even the most demanding' predicts 'diligent.' Assiduous fits. Trap: perfunctory (superficial) is thematically about office work but is the opposite of impressive diligence.

stem: The corporation's annual report, though full of impressive statistics, was ultimately _____, obscuring the company's mounting debts beneath a veneer of soundness.
explain: 'Impressive statistics...obscuring...beneath a veneer' predicts 'seemingly sound but false.' Specious fits. Trap: transparent is the opposite, the very quality the report lacks.

stem: The philosopher's prose, admired by specialists, remains _____ to general readers, who find its dense jargon impenetrable.
explain: 'Dense jargon impenetrable' predicts 'obscure.' Recondite fits. Trap: lucid is the opposite, describing clarity rather than difficulty.

stem: Unlike the party's other candidates, who courted controversy, the newcomer campaigned on a resolutely _____ platform that avoided taking sides on divisive issues.
explain: 'Avoided taking sides on divisive issues' predicts 'unbiased.' Disinterested means impartial. Trap: partisan is nearly the opposite, describing one-sided commitment.

stem: The scholar's argument, though initially dismissed as fringe, has since been _____ by a growing body of archaeological evidence.
explain: 'Though initially dismissed...has since been' signals reversal toward support; predict 'confirmed.' Substantiated means supported with proof. Trap: refuted continues the initial dismissal rather than reflecting the shift signaled by 'since.'

stem: The CEO's memo, meant to reassure employees, was instead full of _____ jargon that left most staff more confused than before.
explain: 'Left most staff more confused' predicts 'muddled.' Turbid means muddy or confused. Trap: transparent is the opposite of what confusing jargon produces.

stem: Though the ambassador's manner was outwardly _____, colleagues who worked closely with her sensed a fierce ambition beneath the calm exterior.
explain: 'Though outwardly X...beneath the calm exterior' means X restates calm; predict 'serene.' Placid fits. Trap: volatile contradicts the stated 'calm exterior.'

stem: The archivist's cataloguing, admired for its _____ precision, accounted for every item in the collection down to the smallest fragment.
explain: 'Every item...down to the smallest fragment' predicts 'extremely careful.' Meticulous fits. Trap: cursory (hasty) is thematically about cataloguing but is the opposite of careful precision.

stem: The negotiations stalled because neither party would compromise, each side remaining stubbornly _____ on every original demand.
explain: 'Stalled...would not compromise' predicts 'unyielding.' Obdurate means stubborn. Trap: tractable (yielding) is thematically about negotiation but is the opposite of refusing to compromise.

stem: The professor's grading was famously _____; a single misplaced comma could cost a student half a letter grade.
explain: 'A single misplaced comma could cost half a grade' predicts 'extremely strict about detail.' Punctilious fits. Trap: lax is the opposite, describing carelessness rather than strictness.

stem: The memoirist's account, while emotionally moving, is widely regarded by historians as _____, riddled with dates and details that never occurred.
explain: 'Riddled with dates and details that never occurred' predicts 'based on false facts.' Fallacious fits. Trap: veracious (truthful) is the opposite, contradicting the fabricated details.

stem: The tribe's oral traditions, passed down for centuries, proved remarkably _____ when compared against archaeological findings uncovered only recently.
explain: 'Proved remarkably...when compared against findings' predicts 'accurate.' Veracious means truthful. Trap: apocryphal (of doubtful authenticity) is thematically about oral tradition but is the opposite of verified.

stem: Unlike his famously taciturn colleagues, the new manager was strikingly _____, striking up conversation with nearly every employee he passed.
explain: 'Striking up conversation with nearly every employee' predicts 'sociable.' Gregarious fits. Trap: reticent (reserved) matches the colleagues described, not the manager's contrasting behavior.

stem: The startup's growth, once _____, slowed dramatically after its main investor withdrew funding.
explain: 'Once X, slowed dramatically after' predicts prior rapid growth. Burgeoning fits. Trap: stagnant describes the later state, not the earlier contrast.

stem: The negotiator's proposal was met with _____ silence, as no one in the room seemed willing to voice either support or objection.
explain: 'Neither support nor objection' predicts 'mixed/uncertain.' Ambivalent fits. Trap: enthusiastic contradicts the described silence and lack of reaction.

stem: The senator's supporters praised his consistency, while critics saw the same trait as mere _____, an inability to adapt to changing circumstances.
explain: 'Inability to adapt' predicts 'stubbornness.' Obduracy fits. Trap: flexibility is the opposite of the inability described.

stem: The chemist's early experiments, dismissed by peers as _____, later formed the foundation of an entirely new field of study.
explain: 'Dismissed...later formed the foundation' signals the early view was doubtful, unlike its eventual importance; predict 'foolish.' Fatuous fits. Trap: seminal describes the later significance, not the original dismissive judgment.

stem: The lawyer's cross-examination was relentlessly _____, its biting, incisive questions forcing the witness to admit inconsistencies in his earlier testimony.
explain: 'Biting, incisive questions forcing the witness to admit inconsistencies' predicts 'sharp and cutting.' Pungent fits this figurative sense (biting, caustic). Trap: desultory (aimless, unfocused) contradicts the effective, targeted questioning described.

stem: Although the art dealer's manner was charming, seasoned collectors regarded his praise of every painting as _____ rather than genuine.
explain: 'Rather than genuine' predicts 'excessive/insincere.' Fulsome fits, meaning so excessive as to be disgusting. Trap: sincere is the opposite, directly contradicted by 'rather than.'

stem: The commission's findings, unsealed after years of official denial, ultimately _____ rumors that critics had long dismissed as baseless conspiracy theories.
explain: 'Long dismissed as baseless...unsealed after denial' signals the rumors turn out true; predict 'confirmed.' Substantiated fits. Trap: dispelled implies the rumors were false, contradicting the reversal of the earlier dismissal.

stem: Despite the coach's reputation for _____ discipline, his players described him privately as remarkably lenient during practice.
explain: 'Despite...privately...lenient' signals contrast; predict 'harsh, strict.' Draconian fits (excessively harsh). Trap: lax matches the actual private behavior, not the public reputation required by 'despite.'

stem: The senator's speech was praised for its _____ clarity, distilling a complicated policy into terms any citizen could understand.
explain: 'Distilling...any citizen could understand' predicts 'clear and convincing.' Cogent fits. Trap: turgid (pompous, swollen) contradicts the described accessibility.

stem: The curator's decision to display the fragments unrestored was praised by purists as _____, though many visitors found the shattered vessels merely confusing.
explain: 'Praised by purists' predicts a positive, defensible word despite visitor confusion; predict 'admirable.' Estimable fits. Trap: capricious implies random whim, undermining the purists' praise.

stem: The philosopher's treatise, for all its apparent rigor, rests on a single _____ premise that, once questioned, causes the entire argument to collapse.
explain: 'Once questioned...entire argument to collapse' predicts 'indefensible.' Untenable fits. Trap: axiomatic (taken for granted) is thematically about premises but implies unquestionable soundness, the opposite of fragility.

stem: The senator's memoir, ostensibly a candid confession, is in fact a carefully _____ document designed to rehabilitate her public image.
explain: 'Ostensibly candid...in fact carefully...designed to rehabilitate' signals contrast to genuine spontaneity; predict 'crafty, not candid.' Disingenuous fits. Trap: artless (without guile) is the opposite, matching the false appearance rather than the reality.

stem: Far from being the _____ figure his enemies portrayed, the reformer's private letters reveal a man tormented by self-doubt.
explain: 'Far from...tormented by self-doubt' signals the public image was the opposite of doubt; predict 'unyielding.' Implacable fits. Trap: irresolute matches the private reality, not the public caricature the sentence asks for.

stem: The committee's report, ostensibly neutral, was in fact so _____ toward the incumbent administration that opposition members refused to sign it.
explain: 'Ostensibly neutral...in fact so X...refused to sign' signals reversal toward bias; predict 'one-sided.' Partisan fits. Trap: disinterested (unbiased) matches the false appearance, not the actual bias revealed.

stem: The critic's praise, though seemingly effusive, was laced with just enough _____ qualification to leave the playwright uncertain whether he had been complimented or condemned.
explain: 'Uncertain whether complimented or condemned' predicts 'unclear in meaning.' Ambiguous fits. Trap: categorical (absolute, unqualified) contradicts the described uncertainty.

stem: What appeared to be the economist's _____ acceptance of the new policy was, colleagues later learned, a calculated silence meant to avoid professional retaliation.
explain: 'Calculated silence' clarifies the earlier word describes unspoken agreement; predict 'silently understood.' Tacit fits. Trap: vociferous (loud) contradicts the described silence.

stem: The biographer resists the temptation to _____ her subject's failures, presenting his cruelty alongside his undeniable genius without softening either.
explain: 'Without softening either' predicts avoidance of 'excusing/minimizing.' Mitigate fits (to lessen the severity of). Trap: exacerbate means to worsen, the opposite error a biographer might commit.

stem: The regime's censors, far from suppressing the poet's work entirely, allowed just enough of it to circulate to seem _____, thereby avoiding the appearance of tyranny.
explain: 'Avoiding the appearance of tyranny' predicts the desired image is 'tolerant.' Liberal fits this sense (tolerant, broad-minded). Trap: despotic is the very impression the regime sought to avoid, the opposite of the intended effect.

stem: The panel's verdict, though framed in the neutral language of scholarship, could not entirely _____ its authors' evident sympathy for the accused.
explain: 'Neutral language...could not entirely X its evident sympathy' predicts the sympathy still showed through despite attempts to hide it; predict 'conceal.' Disguise fits. Trap: betray means to reveal unintentionally, which reverses the required logic of 'could not entirely.'

stem: The senator's rhetoric, for all its surface moderation, was calculated to _____ rather than to genuinely reconcile the party's warring factions.
explain: 'Surface moderation...calculated to X rather than genuinely reconcile' contrasts real reconciliation with a superficial appeasement; predict 'pacify superficially.' Placate fits, since it implies temporary calming rather than true resolution. Trap: alienate contradicts the moderate surface tone entirely.

stem: The translator's rendering, though fluent, arguably _____ the original's deliberate ambiguities into a false clarity the author never intended.
explain: 'False clarity the author never intended' predicts the translation eliminated nuance; predict 'weakens, thins out.' Attenuates fits. Trap: preserves is the opposite, describing fidelity rather than distortion.

stem: The geologist's model, elegant on paper, proved _____ when field data from three separate expeditions contradicted its central predictions.
explain: 'Contradicted its central predictions' predicts 'unable to be defended.' Untenable fits. Trap: corroborated is the opposite of what contradictory data would do to a model.

stem: The ambassador's prolonged silence at the summit struck outside observers as deeply meaningful, though insiders dismissed it as entirely _____, a simple by-product of exhaustion after days of fruitless talks.
explain: 'Insiders dismissed it as entirely X...simple by-product of exhaustion' predicts 'unimportant.' Inconsequential fits. Trap: momentous matches the outside observers' mistaken reading, not the insiders' actual dismissal.

stem: The dissertation's central claim, though hedged in cautious academic prose, is in essence a fairly _____ challenge to decades of settled scholarly consensus.
explain: 'Though hedged in cautious prose...in essence a fairly X challenge to settled consensus' signals the underlying substance is bold despite cautious wording; predict 'daring.' Audacious fits. Trap: diffident matches the cautious prose, not the underlying substance the sentence asks about.

stem: The memoirist's studied avoidance of self-pity gives the narrative an _____ quality rare in accounts of personal tragedy.
explain: 'Studied avoidance of self-pity' predicts 'unshaken, composed.' Imperturbable fits. Trap: maudlin (excessively sentimental) is thematically tied to tragedy but is the opposite of restraint.

stem: The critic contended that the painting's much-discussed 'simplicity' was in fact the product of an almost _____ attention to compositional detail.
explain: 'Simplicity...in fact the product of an almost X attention to detail' signals the simple appearance concealed meticulous effort; predict 'extremely careful.' Punctilious fits. Trap: cursory (hasty) contradicts the described intense attention.

stem: Rather than the wholesale rejection of tradition his critics alleged, the architect's work represents a more _____ engagement, borrowing selectively even as it innovates.
explain: 'Borrowing selectively even as it innovates' predicts 'drawing from varied sources.' Eclectic fits. Trap: categorical (absolute) matches the critics' alleged view the sentence explicitly rejects.

stem: The diplomat's memoir, written decades after the crisis, offers a startlingly _____ account, at odds with the self-serving version he gave at the time.
explain: 'At odds with the self-serving version he gave at the time' predicts a truthful contrast; predict 'genuine.' Unfeigned fits. Trap: guarded (cautious) contradicts the startling openness the sentence describes.

stem: Though the tribunal's ruling was couched in dispassionate legal language that carefully avoided any accusation, its practical effect was nonetheless to _____ the very regime it claimed only to be studying.
explain: 'Carefully avoided any accusation...its practical effect was nonetheless' signals a contrast between the ruling's neutral surface and its real-world impact; predict 'weaken, damage the standing of.' Undermine fits. Trap: sanction (to approve, formally endorse) matches the false appearance of dispassionate neutrality, not the actual damaging effect that 'nonetheless' signals; legitimize, vindicate, and bolster all share that same wrong (approving) direction.

stem: Although the new intern's manner was initially (i)_____, her colleagues soon realized that beneath the shy exterior lay a remarkably (ii)_____ wit.
explain: Solve (i) first: 'shy exterior' signals reticent, not gregarious (opposite) or obsequious (irrelevant). 'Although' then flips expectation: despite shyness, her wit was sharp, so caustic fits; insipid (dull) is the opposite-direction trap, and morose doesn't describe wit.

stem: Economists (i)_____ that a modest interest-rate increase would (ii)_____ inflation without triggering a recession.
explain: (i) needs a verb meaning 'assert a claim'; contend fits, while quibble (argue over trifles) and vacillate (waver) don't suit stating an economic thesis. (ii) must mean 'reduce,' matching the goal of controlling inflation; exacerbate is the opposite-direction trap, proliferate is nonsensical here.

stem: The treaty's vague language did little to (i)_____ further conflict, and the already (ii)_____ peace finally gave way to open war.
explain: War breaking out shows the treaty failed to prevent conflict, so forestall fits; engender (cause) reverses the logic. Since the peace 'gave way,' it must have been weak: tenuous fits, while robust and placid (both suggesting stability) are opposite-direction traps.

stem: The compound's properties proved remarkably (i)_____ under laboratory conditions, remaining stable even as researchers subjected it to (ii)_____ swings in temperature and pressure.
explain: 'Remaining stable' requires immutable (unchangeable); volatile is the direct opposite-meaning trap. 'Swings' implies irregular changes, matching sporadic; homogeneous (uniform) contradicts 'swings,' and innocuous (harmless) misses the point about temperature/pressure changes entirely.

stem: The playwright's early works were marked by (i)_____ ornamentation, but his later plays embraced a (ii)_____ style, stripped of all but the essential lines.
explain: 'Ornamentation' pairs with grandiloquent (bombastic); austere would contradict 'ornamentation,' a placement trap. The contrast word 'but' plus 'stripped... essential' signals austere for (ii); bombastic/verbose reverse the meaning and would fit (i) instead, not (ii).

stem: In tightly knit rural communities, residents tend to be (i)_____, whereas urban anonymity often breeds (ii)_____ among neighbors.
explain: 'Tightly knit' implies sociability, so gregarious fits (i); reticent (reserved) is the opposite trap. 'Whereas' signals contrast with anonymity, which breeds indifference: apathy fits (ii); alacrity (eagerness) and ardor (passion) are wrong-direction traps implying engagement, not isolation.

stem: The museum's new wing was designed to be (i)_____, its bold glass forms clashing intentionally with the (ii)_____ stone facade of the original building.
explain: 'Bold... clashing' signals showiness, so ostentatious fits (i); unassuming is the opposite trap. The old stone facade, by contrast, should be plain: austere fits (ii); luminous (glowing) misdescribes stone, and gregarious (sociable) cannot describe a facade at all.

stem: The witness's testimony was so (i)_____ that the jury reached its verdict quickly, since every detail (ii)_____ perfectly with the physical evidence.
explain: Quick, confident verdicts follow from clear testimony, so lucid fits (i); desultory and ambiguous are opposite-direction traps. 'Perfectly with the evidence' needs agreement: jibe fits (ii); belie (contradict) is the direct opposite trap, and digress is irrelevant to matching evidence.

stem: Given the (i)_____ of profits this quarter, the board urged investors to temper their (ii)_____ about the prospects for a large dividend.
explain: Urging investors to lower expectations implies profits were scarce: paucity fits (i); plethora (excess) is the opposite trap. 'Temper' means to moderate something strong, so ardor (passionate hope) fits (ii); apathy needs no tempering, making it a wrong-direction trap.

stem: The tour guide's knowledge of local history was (i)_____, offering visitors far more detail than the brief (ii)_____ printed in their pamphlets.
explain: 'Far more detail' implies deep learning, so erudite fits (i); vacuous (empty of intelligence) is the opposite trap. The pamphlets' summary must be brief, matching compendium; treatise and tome both imply length, making them wrong-direction traps for (ii).

stem: Critics initially dismissed the poet's fragmented syntax as mere affectation, but subsequent scholars have argued that the seemingly (i)_____ structure in fact (ii)_____ a rigorous underlying logic.
explain: 'Fragmented' and 'dismissed as affectation' match desultory (random); meticulous/lucid already imply order, so they'd need no 'but' contrast. The verb must show the disorder misrepresents hidden rigor: belie fits; exemplify reverses the logic (agreement, not contrast) and negate is the wrong sense.

stem: The central bank's (i)_____ decision to raise interest rates before the data were fully in struck many economists as (ii)_____, particularly once inflation began cooling on its own.
explain: 'Before the data were fully in' signals a hasty decision: precipitate fits; judicious (wise) is the opposite trap. Since inflation cooled 'on its own,' the rate hike wasn't needed: premature fits (ii); warranted is a direct opposite-direction trap pulled straight from the word list.

stem: Because the newly discovered species showed no clear evolutionary link to its neighbors, taxonomists initially treated its classification as (i)_____, pending further genetic analysis that might either (ii)_____ or overturn the tentative placement.
explain: 'Pending further analysis' and 'tentative' require indeterminate (unsettled); immutable/axiomatic both wrongly imply certainty. The analysis could 'either X or overturn' the placement, so (ii) needs the opposite of overturn: substantiate (support); obviate (make unnecessary) and digress don't fit that pairing.

stem: Though the general's early campaigns had earned him a reputation for (i)_____ boldness, his final battle revealed a startling (ii)_____, as he hesitated at the very moment decisive action was required.
explain: 'Reputation for... boldness' needs audacious; craven (cowardly) and wary contradict 'boldness.' 'Though' signals contrast, and 'hesitated' points to irresolution; alacrity (eager speed) is the opposite trap, and audacity wrongly echoes blank (i) instead of contrasting with it.

stem: Anthropologists studying the isolated village noted that its residents remained remarkably (i)_____ to outside influence, preserving customs that neighboring communities had long since (ii)_____ in favor of modern practices.
explain: 'Preserving customs' despite outside contact needs impervious (unaffected); porous and amenable (open to influence) are opposite-direction traps. Neighbors who switched to modern practices must have renounced the old customs: forsworn fits; embraced and venerated wrongly suggest they kept honoring them.

stem: Labor economists have long debated whether automation will (i)_____ traditional manufacturing jobs entirely or merely (ii)_____ them, shifting workers toward higher-skill roles within the same industry.
explain: 'Entirely' replacing jobs needs supersede; bolster (support) and sanction (approve) don't fit elimination. The 'or merely' contrast requires a milder alternative than elimination: redefine fits; supplant is a near-synonym of supersede, creating an illogical redundant pairing, and aggregate is irrelevant.

stem: The composer's late symphonies, once derided as (i)_____ by critics who found their harmonies grating, are now celebrated for a (ii)_____ dissonance that rewards patient listening.
explain: 'Grating' harmonies match cacophonous (harsh-sounding); mellifluous and placid are opposite-direction traps. 'Now celebrated' requires a positive reframing of the same dissonance: compelling (engaging, having force) fits; desultory (aimless) and strident (harsh) merely restate the old negative criticism rather than the new praise.

stem: Skeptics have long (i)_____ the possibility of certain knowledge, arguing that even our most confident perceptions may be (ii)_____ by the limitations of the senses.
explain: Skeptics doubt, so they 'deny' certain knowledge: gainsay fits; substantiate/aver (both affirming) are opposite-direction traps. Sense limitations should weaken perceptions, matching vitiated (impaired); substantiated and bolstered wrongly suggest perceptions are strengthened, not undermined.

stem: Invasive species often (i)_____ rapidly in ecosystems lacking natural predators, a pattern of unchecked growth that can (ii)_____ native populations within a few short seasons.
explain: 'Unchecked growth' requires proliferate; subside and abate (both meaning decrease) are opposite-direction traps. Unchecked invasive growth threatens natives by replacing them: supplant fits; bolster (support) reverses the harm implied, and propitiate (appease) is irrelevant to population dynamics.

stem: The dialect's grammar, though (i)_____ to outsiders, follows internally consistent rules that linguists have painstakingly (ii)_____ over decades of fieldwork.
explain: 'Though' signals contrast with 'internally consistent,' so outsiders must find it hard to grasp: recondite fits; lucid/pellucid (both clear) are opposite-direction traps. Decades of fieldwork should systematize the rules: codified fits; obscured and vitiated both wrongly imply the rules became less clear.

stem: The forger's copies were so (i)_____ that even seasoned curators were initially (ii)_____, mistaking the fakes for authentic masterpieces.
explain: Convincing-but-false copies match meretricious (plausible but specious); execrable and banal describe poor quality, which wouldn't fool experts. 'Mistaking the fakes' shows curators were fooled: duped fits; wary (cautious) and disabused (freed from illusion) both contradict being deceived.

stem: Consumers often display a curious (i)_____ when it comes to saving money: they profess a strong desire to save yet routinely (ii)_____ that intention by making impulsive purchases.
explain: Professing one thing yet doing another signals conflicted feelings: ambivalence fits; resolve (firmness) and probity (honesty) don't capture the contradiction. Impulsive purchases undercut the stated intention, matching belie (contradict); substantiate and bolster wrongly imply the intention is supported.

stem: Though later biographers portrayed the queen as (i)_____, contemporary accounts describe a ruler who was, in private, remarkably (ii)_____ toward her advisors, often overruling their counsel without explanation.
explain: 'Though' contrasts with the private reality, so the public image must be mild: tractable fits (i); obdurate/adamant (both stubborn) already match the private trait and break the contrast. Overruling advisors without explanation needs peremptory; complaisant (eager to please) and tractable reverse the meaning.

stem: Seismologists caution that the fault's long period of (i)_____ should not be mistaken for permanent stability, since even (ii)_____ faults can rupture without warning after centuries of accumulated strain.
explain: A 'period' mistaken for stability implies inactivity: quiescence fits; volatility/turbulence describe active instability, the opposite. 'Even X faults can rupture' needs a word for seemingly inactive ones: dormant fits; restive (unsettled) and volatile both wrongly suggest visible instability already.

stem: Media scholars argue that the algorithm's design, far from being (i)_____ as its engineers claim, actually (ii)_____ users toward increasingly extreme content by rewarding engagement above all else.
explain: Engineers claim neutrality: disinterested (unbiased) fits; contentious and apathetic describe different, irrelevant qualities. 'Far from' signals the opposite is true: the algorithm actively pushes users, matching goad (prod, urge on); dissuade and placate both wrongly imply discouraging extreme content.

stem: The philosopher's argument, for all its apparent rigor, rests on a premise so (i)_____ that once exposed, the entire edifice of reasoning built upon it appears not merely flawed but (ii)_____.
explain: 'For all its apparent rigor' but ultimately flawed points to specious (seemingly sound, actually not); axiomatic/cogent both wrongly imply real soundness. 'Not merely flawed but' demands an intensified negative: untenable fits; cogent and judicious are positive, opposite-direction traps.

stem: That the policy succeeded in curbing inflation is, upon closer analysis, less a triumph of monetary (i)_____ than a fortuitous byproduct of falling global energy prices, a distinction the finance minister has been curiously reluctant to (ii)_____.
explain: 'Triumph of monetary X' needs a word about effectiveness: efficacy fits; exigency (urgency) and frugality (thrift) are wrong meanings. A minister reluctant to admit a distinction implies withholding a fact: divulge fits; disseminate is a near-miss (spreading info generally, not revealing a secret), and embellish is unrelated.

stem: To call the memoir 'confessional' is to commit a category error: rather than genuine self-exposure, the narrator's disclosures are so carefully staged that what reads as vulnerability is in fact a (i)_____ performance, its seeming candor no less (ii)_____ than the persona it claims to strip away.
explain: 'Carefully staged' vulnerability implies calculated insincerity: disingenuous fits; guileless/artless (both meaning honest) are opposite-direction traps. 'No less X than the persona' means the candor is equally artificial: affected fits; unfeigned and veracious (both genuine) contradict the claim of staged performance.

stem: Evolutionary biologists have grown (i)_____ of explanations that attribute every anatomical feature to adaptive advantage, noting that some traits may be merely (ii)_____ byproducts of developmental constraints rather than targets of natural selection.
explain: Growing cautious about overreaching explanations needs wary; gullible/ingenuous (both naive) are opposite-direction traps for scientists exercising caution. 'Merely X byproducts... rather than targets of selection' requires an incidental, non-essential sense: extraneous fits; cardinal (foremost) and causal (implying intentional selection) both reverse the meaning.

stem: The critic's insistence that the sculpture's crude finish was a deliberate aesthetic choice rather than technical failure strikes many as (i)_____, an attempt to (ii)_____ what is more plausibly explained by the artist's limited skill.
explain: An unconvincing defense of a claim fits specious; apposite (fitting) and felicitous (well-chosen) wrongly praise the critic's reasoning. The critic is inflating the sculpture's significance beyond its likely cause: aggrandize fits; denigrate and disparage (both meaning belittle) are opposite-direction traps.

stem: Revisionist historians have challenged the (i)_____ view that the reform was universally popular, marshaling archival evidence that ordinary citizens greeted the new laws with far more (ii)_____ than official chronicles ever acknowledged.
explain: Revisionists challenge an established, unquestioned view: hallowed (venerated) fits; heterodox/iconoclastic describe the revisionists' own position, not the old view they're attacking. Citizens' true reaction, hidden by chronicles, must be negative: antipathy fits; alacrity and deference are opposite-direction traps implying welcome.

stem: Negotiators who appear entirely (i)_____ to the other side's concerns often achieve worse outcomes than those who feign flexibility, since intransigence, however strategically calculated, tends to (ii)_____ reciprocal goodwill rather than extract concessions.
explain: 'Intransigence' later in the sentence confirms the negotiators are inflexible: implacable fits; amenable/complaisant (both agreeable) contradict intransigence. Intransigence undermining goodwill 'rather than extract concessions' needs vitiate (corrupt/impair); engender (create) is the opposite trap, and foment (incite) doesn't collocate with 'goodwill.'

stem: The alloy's newfound resistance to corrosion is not, as the manufacturer's marketing (i)_____, evidence of a fundamentally novel compound, but rather the predictable result of a well-understood surface treatment that engineers have long considered (ii)_____ rather than groundbreaking.
explain: Marketing making a claim needs avers (affirms); disabuses (corrects a misconception) and gainsays (denies) would mean the marketing undercuts itself, illogical. 'Rather than groundbreaking' needs its opposite: mundane fits; novel and singular both mean new/unique, contradicting the intended contrast.

stem: The regime's officials insisted that dissent had been all but eliminated, yet the sheer (i)_____ of underground pamphlets circulating in the capital belied their claim, suggesting that opposition, far from vanishing, had merely grown more (ii)_____ in its methods.
explain: 'Belied their claim' of elimination requires abundant evidence: plethora fits; paucity/dearth (both scarcity) would actually support the regime's claim, the opposite of what's needed. Surviving opposition that avoided detection must have gone underground: covert fits; overt and brazen (both open) contradict evading the regime.

stem: What distinguishes the elegy from mere lament is its refusal to remain (i)_____; even as the poet mourns, the verse strains toward a kind of consolation, its grief (ii)_____ by flashes of hard-won affirmation.
explain: 'Mere lament' and 'refusal to remain' point to a purely mournful state being resisted: plaintive fits; jubilant/ebullient (both joyful) can't be what a poem 'refuses to remain' amid mourning. 'Flashes of affirmation' should lessen the grief: mitigated fits; exacerbated and compounded both mean worsened, the opposite.

stem: Conservationists once believed that top predators were (i)_____ to ecosystem health, their removal producing no lasting effects. Field studies over the past decades have (ii)_____ this assumption, revealing that when wolves vanished from a region, deer populations exploded and overgrazing left the landscape strikingly (iii)_____.
explain: Solve (i) first: 'no lasting effects' from removal implies predators were non-essential, so extraneous fits; cardinal/inherent wrongly suggest necessity. Since studies found real effects, they disproved the old belief: refuted fits. Overgrazing implies a dried-out land: desiccated fits; pristine/luminous are opposite-direction traps.

stem: Proponents of the trade agreement argue that removing tariffs will (i)_____ domestic industries to compete more efficiently, forcing them to abandon (ii)_____ practices that have long shielded them from foreign rivals. Critics counter that without protection, many smaller firms will be unable to survive the transition and will instead (iii)_____.
explain: 'Forcing them to abandon' signals a push, so goad fits (i); placate/mollify (soothe) contradict forcing change. Practices that shielded firms from rivals are inward-looking: insular fits (ii). Firms 'unable to survive' must fail: founder fits (iii); flourish/burgeon (thrive) are opposite-direction traps.

stem: The general's memoirs present his decision to retreat as a masterstroke of strategy, but contemporary letters suggest the retreat was in fact (i)_____, undertaken in a moment of panic rather than calculation. His officers, for their part, were too (ii)_____ to challenge his account publicly, and so the myth of tactical genius went largely (iii)_____ for over a century.
explain: 'Panic rather than calculation' needs a hasty sense: precipitate fits (i); judicious/sage (both wise) are opposite-direction traps. Officers staying silent implies deference: obsequious fits (ii); contentious/truculent (combative) contradict silence. A myth that persisted 'for over a century' went unquestioned: unchallenged fits (iii).

stem: The building's facade, with its rows of identical windows and unadorned concrete, exemplifies an (i)_____ style that eschews ornamentation in favor of pure function. Critics who find such structures cold nonetheless concede that the design's very (ii)_____ makes it remarkably adaptable, since the interior can be reconfigured without regard to decorative constraints. What the style sacrifices in warmth, then, it arguably (iii)_____ in versatility.
explain: 'Unadorned' and 'eschews ornamentation' require austere; bombastic/florid (both ornate) are opposite-direction traps. The 'since' clause explains adaptability as a result of having no decorative constraints, i.e. the design's restrained plainness: sobriety fits (ii); grandiosity (showy excess) is the opposite of the austere style already established, and immutability (unchangeability) directly contradicts 'adaptable.' 'Sacrifices... but arguably X in versatility' needs a gain: compensates fits; forfeits/relinquishes (both meaning lose) reverse the logic.

stem: Early behaviorists were (i)_____ of any explanation that invoked unobservable mental states, insisting that psychology should confine itself strictly to measurable behavior. Later cognitive scientists found this position too (ii)_____, arguing that ignoring internal mental processes left huge swaths of human experience unexplained. Today most researchers occupy a middle ground, treating the old debate as largely (iii)_____.
