explain: Rejecting unobservable mental states signals dismissiveness: dismissive fits (i); credulous/amenable (open, accepting) contradict rejecting explanations. 'Too X' followed by a complaint about narrowness needs insular fits (ii); eclectic (broad-ranging) is the opposite trap. A 'middle ground' treats the old debate as no longer live: defunct fits (iii); cardinal/pervasive (still central) are opposite traps.

stem: Astronomers were initially (i)_____ about the signal's origin, since natural phenomena can produce similarly patterned radio bursts. Follow-up observations, however, ruled out every known astrophysical explanation, lending unexpected (ii)_____ to the more speculative hypothesis that the signal was artificial. Even so, most researchers remain (iii)_____, noting that ruling out known explanations is not the same as confirming an exotic one.
explain: Doubting a claim before evidence needs wary; credulous/gullible (easily convinced) contradict initial caution. Ruling out natural causes gives new support to a speculative idea: credence fits (ii); opprobrium (disgrace) and skepticism reverse the meaning. 'Even so... noting' signals continued caution rather than belief: skeptical fits (iii); credulous/convinced are opposite-direction traps.

stem: Some economists contend that rising inequality is largely (i)_____, a natural byproduct of technological change that no policy can fully reverse. Others insist the trend is far more (ii)_____, shaped by specific tax and labor policies that could, in principle, be revised. This disagreement matters because the first view counsels resignation, while the second (iii)_____ reform.
explain: 'No policy can fully reverse' means inevitable: ineluctable fits (i); avoidable/negotiable contradict 'cannot reverse.' 'Far more X, shaped by policies that could... be revised' needs changeable: mutable fits (ii); immutable/intractable (both fixed) are opposite traps. The second view supports action: champions fits (iii); forestalls/obviates (prevent, negate) reverse the meaning.

stem: Urban planners once assumed that dense housing necessarily produced (i)_____ neighborhoods, cramped and unpleasant places to live. Data from several redesigned districts have (ii)_____ this belief, showing that density paired with good design can create vibrant, walkable communities. Even skeptics now admit that the old equation of density with decline was (iii)_____.
explain: 'Cramped and unpleasant' matches sordid; salubrious (healthful)/pristine (uncorrupted) are opposite traps. New data contradicting the old belief needs belied; corroborated/substantiated (both supporting) reverse the logic. An equation now admitted to be wrong needs fallacious; cogent/veracious (both sound) are opposite-direction traps.

stem: The skeptic's challenge is not that our beliefs are occasionally mistaken—a claim no one would (i)_____—but that we can never possess sufficient grounds to distinguish a mistaken belief from a true one, rendering the very notion of justified belief (ii)_____. Defenders of common sense reply that such radical doubt, however (iii)_____ in the seminar room, collapses the moment one must act in the world, where practical certainty suffices.
explain: A claim 'no one would' contest is uncontroversial: gainsay (dispute) fits (i); aver/substantiate wrongly mean affirm. Inability to distinguish true from false beliefs undermines the whole concept: untenable fits (ii). 'However X in the seminar room, collapses... in the world' needs a concession of theoretical persuasiveness: cogent fits (iii); untenable (reused) and specious both contradict the concession.

stem: The paper's central claim—that minimum-wage increases have historically produced negligible job losses—rests on a data set so (i)_____ that even sympathetic reviewers hesitate to draw strong conclusions from it. This has not stopped advocates from (ii)_____ the finding as definitive proof of a settled question, an overreach that has done more to (iii)_____ the broader debate than to resolve it.
explain: 'Even sympathetic reviewers hesitate' implies weak data: attenuated fits (i); copious/aggregate (abundant, comprehensive) are opposite traps. Advocates overselling a weak finding need touting (promoting); disparaging/discrediting (undermining) reverse the meaning. An overreach that worsens rather than resolves debate needs exacerbate (iii); mitigate/ameliorate (improve) are opposite-direction traps.

stem: It would be a mistake to read the painter's late turn toward abstraction as a repudiation of her earlier representational work; the two modes, on close inspection, share a common concern with texture and light that renders any strict periodization (i)_____. What changed was not her underlying sensibility but her willingness to let form become fully (ii)_____ from recognizable subject matter, a shift that struck early critics as (iii)_____ but now appears as the logical culmination of tendencies present from the start.
explain: Shared concerns across periods undermine a strict dividing line: untenable fits (i); axiomatic/warranted wrongly validate periodization. Form separating from subject matter needs autonomous (independent); contiguous (touching) and commensurate (proportional) are wrong-meaning traps. A shift critics saw as a break, now seen as logical, needs anomalous (iii); apposite/inherent contradict the 'struck critics as' framing.

stem: Popular accounts of neuroplasticity often (i)_____ its therapeutic potential, implying that sufficient willpower can rewire any circuit regardless of age or injury severity. The underlying research, more (ii)_____ in its claims, suggests that plasticity is real but highly constrained by developmental windows and lesion location—constraints that popularizers, eager for an uplifting narrative, routinely (iii)_____.
explain: Implying limitless rewiring inflates the claim: aggrandize fits (i); denigrate/disparage (belittle) reverse the meaning. Research that acknowledges 'constrained by' factors is hedged: qualified fits (ii); categorical (absolute) and grandiloquent (bombastic) are opposite-direction traps. Popularizers chasing an 'uplifting narrative' ignore constraints: dismiss fits (iii); substantiate/stipulate (support, specify) reverse the logic.

stem: Historians who treat the revolution as the inevitable culmination of decades of economic grievance risk a kind of retrospective (i)_____, reading backward from the outcome to construct a narrative of inevitability that contemporaries, buffeted by contingent events they could not foresee, would scarcely have recognized. A more (ii)_____ account would restore the genuine uncertainty of the moment, acknowledging that the revolution might easily have (iii)_____ had a handful of decisions gone differently.
explain: Reading inevitability backward is determinism; contingency/spontaneity describe the opposite (unpredictability), what critics want restored. A corrective account grounded in evidence, not backward assumption, needs empirical; dogmatic/doctrinaire (both rigidly opinionated) are opposite traps. 'Might easily have X had decisions gone differently' implies failure: foundered fits; prevailed/triumphed (succeeded) are opposite-direction traps.

stem: The claim that scientific consensus is merely a reflection of social power, rather than a reasonably reliable guide to truth, proves too much: if taken seriously, it would (i)_____ the very sociological analysis used to make the claim, since that analysis is itself a product of social forces and would therefore be no less (ii)_____ than the science it critiques. The self-refuting character of strong social-constructivism has led even sympathetic critics to (iii)_____ its more sweeping formulations while retaining its useful cautions about bias and institutional interest.
explain: Applying the claim to itself would undermine its own analysis: vitiate fits (i); substantiate/bolster (strengthen) reverse the self-refuting logic. Being 'no less X than the science it critiques' means equally suspect: specious fits (ii); cogent/veracious (sound) contradict the parallel. Critics rejecting the 'sweeping formulations' while keeping useful parts need repudiate; embrace/champion (accept) reverse the meaning.

stem: Central bankers walk a narrow path: tighten too aggressively and they risk (i)_____ a recession that need not have occurred; tighten too little and they risk allowing inflation to become (ii)_____, embedding itself in wage expectations in ways that are far costlier to unwind later. The committee's recent statement, studiously (iii)_____ on which risk it now judges greater, has left markets guessing at its true intentions.
explain: 'Tighten too aggressively' risks causing a recession: precipitating fits (i); forestalling/mitigating (preventing) reverse the danger described. Inflation that embeds itself and is 'costlier to unwind' is entrenched: inveterate fits (ii); transient/ephemeral (short-lived) are opposite traps. A statement leaving markets 'guessing' is vague: equivocal fits (iii); categorical/explicit (clear) contradict the guessing.

stem: Translators of the epic have long faced a dilemma: a version faithful to the original's syntax often reads as (i)_____ in English, its inverted clauses and suspended verbs alien to the target language's rhythms, while a version smoothed into idiomatic English risks (ii)_____ precisely those formal peculiarities that made the original distinctive. The best translations, rather than resolving this tension, (iii)_____ it, letting the strangeness of the source language show through without sacrificing readability.
explain: 'Inverted clauses... alien to the rhythms' describes twisted, hard-to-follow prose: tortuous fits (i); lucid/pellucid (clear) are opposite traps. Smoothing risks weakening the original's distinctive traits: attenuating fits (ii); preserving/bolstering (strengthen) reverse the risk described. 'Rather than resolving... X it' explicitly rules out resolve, so sustain fits (iii); obviate (make unnecessary) misses the sense, and resolve directly contradicts the stem's own wording.

stem: Climate models that rely exclusively on historical data risk a subtle circularity: because the data were generated under conditions that no longer strictly hold, projections built upon them may be internally (i)_____ yet externally (ii)_____, accurately extrapolating trends that the changing system itself is in the process of (iii)_____.
explain: 'Internally X yet externally Y' requires a contrast: logically sound within its own framework needs cogent (i); specious/fallacious already describe unsoundness, breaking the 'yet' contrast. Externally, applied to a changed world, the projections are misleading: specious fits (ii). A system 'in the process of' replacing its own old trends needs superseding (iii); sustaining/perpetuating (continuing) reverse the meaning.

stem: Utilitarian critics of rights-based ethics charge that talk of inviolable rights is little more than moral (i)_____, a rhetorically potent but analytically empty gesture that forecloses the very cost-benefit reasoning that, in their view, should govern hard cases. Defenders respond that this charge itself (ii)_____ what rights are meant to do: not to settle every calculation but to (iii)_____ certain outcomes from consideration altogether, regardless of aggregate benefit.
explain: 'Analytically empty' matches platitude (stale, hollow phrase); tenet/precept both imply substantive doctrine, contradicting 'empty.' A charge that misrepresents rights' true purpose needs belies; substantiates/affirms (support) reverse the criticism. Rights meant to exclude outcomes 'regardless of aggregate benefit' need proscribe (forbid); sanction/condone (permit, overlook) are opposite-direction traps.

stem: Language purists who campaign against neologisms and borrowed idioms often assume that linguistic change is a form of (i)_____, a corruption of some earlier, more correct state of the language. Historical linguists find this assumption (ii)_____, pointing out that every 'pure' language they can identify was itself the product of centuries of borrowing and drift, such that the purists' golden age is, on inspection, (iii)_____.
explain: 'A corruption' matches adulteration; refinement/embellishment both imply improvement, the opposite. Linguists debunking the assumption need fallacious; cogent/axiomatic (sound, self-evident) reverse the criticism. A 'golden age' shown never to have existed is illusory: specious fits; veracious (true) and extant (existing) both wrongly affirm its reality.

stem: Early reports linking the supplement to improved longevity relied on observational data plagued by an obvious confound: people who take supplements tend to be wealthier and more health-conscious to begin with, a fact that should have made researchers far more (i)_____ about causal claims than they were. When a randomized trial finally (ii)_____ the supposed benefit, finding no effect once confounders were controlled for, the popular press had already spent a decade (iii)_____ the substance as a near-miracle cure.
explain: An obvious confound should prompt caution: wary fits (i); credulous/gullible (naive acceptance) are opposite traps. A trial 'finding no effect' disproves the benefit: refuted fits (ii); substantiated/confirmed reverse the finding. Press promotion as a 'miracle cure' needs touting (iii); disparaging/denigrating (criticizing) contradict the enthusiastic coverage described.

stem: Foreign aid skeptics argue that large transfers to developing economies often prove (i)_____, propping up inefficient institutions that would otherwise be forced to reform, and thereby (ii)_____ the very development the aid was meant to accelerate. Proponents counter that this argument, while not without merit in specific cases, has been (iii)_____ into a blanket indictment of aid that the empirical record, showing real gains in health and education outcomes, does not support.
explain: Propping up inefficient institutions works against the aid's goal: counterproductive fits (i); salutary/beneficent (beneficial) are opposite traps. Slowing the development aid was meant to accelerate needs impeding (ii); facilitating/engendering (creating) reverse the harm. An argument overgeneralized 'into a blanket indictment' beyond the evidence needs extrapolated (iii); qualified/tempered (narrowed) contradict overgeneralization.

stem: Critics who praise the director's long takes as evidence of formal daring sometimes overlook a simpler explanation: budget constraints made elaborate coverage impossible, and necessity, not aesthetic conviction, (i)_____ many of the choices now celebrated as visionary. This is not to say the films are therefore (ii)_____; a constraint skillfully exploited can produce genuine art, but the critical tendency to read every limitation as intention risks (iii)_____ a coherent aesthetic philosophy where there was often only improvisation.
explain: Necessity producing choices requires engendered (caused); obviated/negated (made unnecessary, canceled) don't fit 'necessity... the choices.' 'This is not to say... therefore X' with 'genuine art' following signals a denial of a negative quality: derivative fits (ii); singular/original are opposite-direction traps. Falsely crediting improvisation with philosophy needs imputing (iii); disavowing/abjuring (rejecting) reverse the meaning.

stem: The instrument's readings, though remarkably precise, are not thereby (i)_____; precision describes only the consistency of repeated measurements, not their correspondence to the quantity actually being measured, and a systematically miscalibrated device can produce results that are precise yet uniformly (ii)_____. Engineers who conflate the two properties risk (iii)_____ confidence in numbers that are, in the relevant sense, simply wrong.
explain: 'Not thereby X' after granting precision requires the distinct concept of accuracy: veracious fits (i); precise/meticulous merely restate the given premise instead of addressing accuracy. Miscalibration produces consistent but wrong results: aberrant fits (ii); veracious/exact (accurate) contradict 'miscalibrated.' Wrongly high confidence in bad numbers needs misplacing (iii); forfeiting/tempering (reducing) imply appropriately lower confidence, the opposite.

stem: To describe the uprising as 'spontaneous' is to accept, uncritically, the colonial administration's own (i)_____ narrative, one crafted precisely to deny the years of organized grievance that preceded it and thereby (ii)_____ any suggestion that the unrest reflected legitimate political demands rather than mere disorder. Archival records recently unearthed by historians (iii)_____ this official account, documenting months of clandestine meetings and coordinated planning that the administration had every incentive to suppress.
explain: A narrative 'crafted precisely to deny' organized grievance is deliberately misleading: disingenuous fits (i); guileless/artless (honest) reverse the meaning. Denying grievance in order to prevent a suggestion of legitimacy needs forestall (ii); engender/substantiate (create, support) reverse the intent. Records showing planning the administration denied contradict the official story: belie fits (iii); substantiate/bolster (support) reverse the finding.

stem: Formalist judges insist that legal texts have a single determinate meaning recoverable through careful reading alone, a position critics dismiss as (i)_____ given how often equally careful readers of the same statute reach opposite conclusions. Yet the opposite extreme—that legal texts are so radically (ii)_____ that judges merely impose their preferences under cover of interpretation—fares little better, since it cannot explain why certain readings are recognized across the profession as clearly wrong. A more defensible position (iii)_____ these poles, treating interpretation as constrained but not mechanical.
explain: Careful readers disagreeing undermines the claim of single determinate meaning: specious fits (i); cogent/axiomatic (sound, self-evident) reverse the criticism. Texts so open that judges 'merely impose preferences' need indeterminate (ii); immutable/axiomatic (fixed) contradict 'radically X.' A position between the two extremes needs mediates (iii); polarizes/radicalizes (extremes) are opposite-direction traps.
